newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan asks for panel to index benefits, taxes.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan asks for panel to index benefits, taxes.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Thursday called for the creation of an independent commission to determine annual cost-of-living increases for federal benefit programmes and tax brackets.

In prepared testimony to the Senate Finance Committee, Greenspan argued that the Consumer Price Index, which is currently used as the basis for cost-of-living changes, overstates inflation by 0.5 to 1.5 percentage points a year.
Greenspan's prepared testimony dwelt entirely on the CPI bias issue. He did not comment on current economic conditions.

Greenspan was one of the first -- and perhaps most influential -- of policy-makers who contend that the CPI is flawed and that the government is losing money by continuing to use it as an index for its programmes.
Millions of Americans, from retirees receiving Social Security benefits to taxpayers, would be affected by any change in the way the government calculates the cost-of-living.
Greenspan argued that the creation of a national commission, which he first proposed two years ago, would not be the "political fix" that some critics charge.
According to the Fed chairman, leaving things as they are now would be tantamount to a political fix because of the widespread agreement that the CPI overstates the actual cost-of-living.

"There is almost a 100 percent probability that we are overcompensating the average Social Security recipient for increases in the cost-of-living, and almost a 100 percent probability that we are causing the inflation-adjusted burden of the income tax system to decline more rapidly than I presume the Congress intends," he said.
"On this issue, we should let evidence, not politics, drive policy," the Fed chief said.

Besides calling for the creation of a national commission, Greenspan also backed increased funding for the Labour Department's Bureau of Labour Statistics so that it could further improve the CPI to make it more accurate.
Greenspan said the BLS should first tackle problems with the CPI that can be addressed quickly, within the next year.
But he added: "Even if the BLS moves aggressively, some upward bias will almost surely remain in the CPI, at least for the next several years."
A panel appointed by the Senate Finance Committee recently concluded that the CPI overstates inflation by 1.1 percentage points a year.
Greenspan said independent Fed research supports that finding and shows that the upward bias in the CPI results in an understatement of productivity in the service sector.

Greenspan said that the new commission he proposed would examine the evidence on changes in the cost-of-living "on a periodic basis" and estimate the bias in the CPI to provide a more accurate calculation for the government.
